what_its_for: Dabrafenib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of melanoma (skin cancer), non-small cell lung cancer, and thyroid cancer that have spread to other parts of the body. It works only in patients whose cancer has a specific gene change called a 'BRAF V600 mutation.' Your doctor will test your cancer to make sure this medicine is right for you. It is often used together with another medicine called trametinib.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsules whole with a full glass of water. Do NOT open, crush, or chew the capsules. Take dabrafenib on an EMPTY STOMACH — either at least 1 hour BEFORE eating or at least 2 hours AFTER eating. Take your two daily doses about 12 hours apart (for example, 8 AM and 8 PM) to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Try to take it at the same times every day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 150 mg (two 75 mg capsules) taken by mouth TWICE a day. Your doctor may change your dose if you have side effects. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed — do not change it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if your next scheduled dose is more than 6 hours away. If your next dose is less than 6 hours away, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store dabrafenib capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the capsules in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect them from moisture and heat. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of drug in your body and cause more side effects. Avoid prolonged sun exposure — dabrafenib can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Use sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and avoid tanning beds. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine — it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Tell your doctor about ALL other medications, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, especially St. John's Wort, as many drugs can interact with dabrafenib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: fever (temperature of 101.3°F or higher), especially with chills, sweating, or feeling very ill (this could be a serious reaction called pyrexia); new skin growths, sores, warts, or changes in moles (this medicine can cause new skin cancers); unusual bleeding or bruising; vision changes such as blurred vision or seeing halos; chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling in your legs (possible heart or blood clot problems); severe headache, confusion, or weakness (possible brain swelling); signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; muscle pain, dark-colored urine, or decreased urination (possible kidney problems); or any unusual or severe symptoms that worry you.
when_it_works: Most patients start to see some benefit within a few weeks to months of starting treatment. However, everyone responds differently. Do not stop taking this medicine just because you feel well or do not notice immediate changes — cancer medicines often work gradually. Keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can check how well the medicine is working through scans and lab tests.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT take dabrafenib if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective non-hormonal birth control (since dabrafenib can make hormonal birth control less effective) during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Men: Use condoms during sex while taking this medicine and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose if your partner could become pregnant. Pediatric patients: This medicine is generally not approved for children, though your doctor may discuss special situations. Older adults (65+): No specific dose changes are needed, but older patients should be monitored carefully for side effects. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
